彼得·奥特曼的研究中心进一步推进了家族裔大脑的3D 映射，研究人员开发出4D 照相机，可以测量线圈中不同组织的结构，这有助于了解前沿医学信息。

搜索结果显示，对于发育时间点来说，刺激率不同和组织类型表现出相关的变化，包括神经元会变成更密集的形状。就像人类中大脑中神经元密度增加的时期一样，不同类型的组织对刺激的频率有不同的响应，显示出组织单元活动的非凡形态特异性。这些发现表明，测量工具可以用来获得广泛的神经发育信息，比如神经元密度的变化或神经活动的异型变化。

摘 要：大脑发育过程中刺激响应的多样化是由组织类型决定的，施加到组织的刺激率会不同，这反过来会影响神经元响应的多种多样。这些结果基于来自3D 照相机的数据，对于发育时间的特定建模而对神经元活动中信息进行推断。大型动物神经系统的问卷调查发现，刺激率与特定神经发育信息的相关性在发育时间内各不相同。包括神经元变密集的形状形状的肌肉、目标和中西部的研究展示了不同的组织相对刺激率响应的形态特异性。这表明测量工具可以用来获得广泛的神经发育信息。

mass.## 2 Problem Formulation

### 2.1 System Description

Consider an uncertain linear time-invariant (LTI) system evolving over a finite horizon of length $T$, described by

$$ x_{t+1} = Ax_t + Bu_t + w_t, \quad y_t = Hx_t + v_t,  \tag{1} $$

where $x_t \in \mathbb{R}^{n_x}$, $u_t \in \mathbb{R}^{n_u}$ and $y_t \in \mathbb{R}^{n_y}$. We assume the initial system state $x_0$, the disturbances $w_0, \ldots, w_{T-1}$ and the measurement noise $v_0, \ldots, v_{T-1}$ are random variables distributed according to a joint distribution $\mathbb{P}^*$. This distribution is unknown but assumed to lie in a given compact set $\mathcal{P}$. We define finite horizon trajectories as $x := \text{col}(x_0, \ldots, x_T) \in \mathbb{R}^{N_x}$; $u := \text{col}(u_0, \ldots, u_{T-1}) \in \mathbb{R}^{N_u}$; $w := \text{col}(x_0, w_0, \ldots, w_{T-1}) \in \mathbb{R}^{N_x}$, $y := \text{col}(y_0, \ldots, y_{T-1}) \in \mathbb{R}^{N_y}$, and $v := \text{col}(v_0, \ldots, v_{T-1}) \in \mathbb{R}^{N_y}$, where $N_x := (T+1)n_x$, $N_u := Tn_u$, and $N_y := Tn_y$. On a finite horizon, the system (1) can then be expressed in terms of linear causal mappings between trajectories as

$$ x = Fu + Gw, \quad y = Cx + v,  \tag{2} $$

where $F$ and $G$ are block lower triangular Toeplitz matrices and $C$ is a rectangular diagonal matrix. They can be routinely constructed from matrices $A, B$, and $H$.

### 2.2 Controller Parameterisation

We parameterise control inputs as causal affine mappings from _purified_ outputs (Ben-Tal et al., 2006). To this end, we first introduce a fictitious LTI system without disturbances and measurement noise, described by

$$ \hat{x}_0 = 0, \quad \hat{x}_{t+1} = A\hat{x}_t + Bu_t, \quad \hat{y}_t = H\hat{x}_t.  \tag{3} $$

A purified output is defined as $\eta_t := y_t - \hat{y}_t$. Finite horizon trajectories corresponding to (3) are defined as $\hat{x} := \text{col}(\hat{x}_0, \ldots, \hat{x}_T) \in \mathbb{R}^{N_x}$, $\hat{y} := \text{col}(\hat{y}_0, \ldots, \hat{y}_{T-1}) \in \mathbb{R}^{N_y}$, and $\eta := \text{col}(\eta_0, \ldots, \eta_{T-1}) \in \mathbb{R}^{N_y}$. Then, the controller parameterisation is given by

$$ u = K\eta + g, \tag{4} $$

where $g \in \mathbb{R}^{N_u}$ and

$$ K := \begin{pmatrix} K_{0,0} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ K_{1,0} & K_{1,1} & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ K_{T-1,0} & \cdots & K_{T-1,T-1} & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \sum_{i=1}^T L_i \begin{pmatrix} K_{i,-1} \\ K_{i,-1} \\ \vdots \\ K_{i-1} \\ K_{i-1} \\ \vdots \\ K_{i-1} \\ K_{i-1} \end{pmatrix} R_i. $$

The left and right factors $L_i$ and $R_i$ are straightforward to construct and not displayed explicitly for reasons of space. The block matrix between them is denoted by $K_i$. We use $\mathcal{K}$ to denote the subset of $\mathbb{R}^{N_u \times N_y}$ that consists of all block lower triangular matrices that correspond to this parameterisation $1$. Based on (4), we can express the input and state trajectories of the LTI system (2) as

$$ u = K(CGw + v) + g, \quad x = FK(CGw + v) + Fg + Gw, $$

with an affine dependence on $(K, g)$. This ensures that the minimisation of a convex function of $(x, u)$ is convex.

## 2.3 Control Problem

We aim to synthesise output feedback controllers in the form of (4) that minimise the worst-case expected regret incurred by them over all distributions in the ambiguity set $\mathcal{P}$. Considering a quadratic cost given by

$$ J(u, w) := x^\top J_x x + u^\top J_u u  \tag{5} $$

where $J_x \in \mathbb{S}^{N_x}_+$ and $J_u \in \mathbb{S}^{N_u}_+$, we can define the regret incurred by an input sequence $u$ with respect to a benchmark policy $u^*$ as

$$ J(u, w) - J(u^*, w),  \tag{6} $$

where $u^*$ possibly depends on $w$ or $v$. In general, a benchmark is chosen as one that yields superior performance but is not implementable in practice. In this work, we choose the benchmark as

$$ u^* = \underset{u \in \mathbb{R}^{N_u}}{\text{argmin}} J(u, w) = K^* w, \tag{7} $$

where $K^* := -(J_u + F^T J_x F)^{-1} F^T J_x G$, and it has knowledge of the disturbance realisations at the outset. Other benchmark policies considered in the literature include, e.g. noncausal output feedback control that is optimal in an $\mathcal{H}_2$ sense (Hajar et al., 2023), and a benchmark that has knowledge of the underlying distributions (Cho and Yang, 2024) and is used to define the ex-ante regret (Poursoltani et al., 2024). The optimality of $u^*$ in (6) allows us to express the regret in a quadratic form as

$$ J(u, w) - J(u^*(w), w) = (u - K^* w)^\top D(u - K^* w)  \tag{8} $$

for any input sequence $u \in \mathbb{R}^{N_u}$, where $D := J_u + F^\top J_x F$. Therefore, based on the parameterisation (4), we denote the regret as $\mathcal{R}(K, g, w, v) := K(\eta + g, w) - J(K^* w, w)$

$$ = \left\|(KCG-K^* K) \begin{pmatrix} w \\ v \end{pmatrix} - g\right\|_D^2. $$

1. As shown in the literature, e.g. (Hadjiyannis et al., 2011; Taskesen et al., 2023), (4) is equivalent to the parameterisation $u = My + s$, where $M \in \mathbb{K}$ and $s \in \mathbb{R}^{N_u}$. Still, the former may be preferred in terms of implementation, as the latter requires a parameter transformation to ensure linear dependence of $x$ and $u$ on decision variables and then possibly large-scale matrix inversion to recover $(M, s)$.
